Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The fiery leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah militant movement assured Lebanon on Monday that his movement will cooperate in the country's political life. Supporters carry posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah. Hassan Nasrallah said: "We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone." Nasrallah spoke a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman the country's president after a six-month vacancy in the position. Nasrallah, speaking at a packed stadium, told his followers: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese." He said Sleiman's election "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start." "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs, we are both in front of two choices; either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon and we prefer the second choice." The parliament had tried 19 times to vote on a new president, but failed because of disagreements over how to share power in a new Cabinet. Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a deal last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that pushed the country to the brink of civil war, and paved the way for Sleiman's election. The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government in which the Cabinet would be comprised of 30 posts -- 16 for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition and three set aside for the president to nominate. The seat allocation had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure it had the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power. In exchange for the veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest that has paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006. In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and to the Arab League for helping broker the deal. Sleiman was the consensus candidate, and is viewed as a neutral party by Lebanon's political factions. The nation's previous presidents have been seen as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. In his 10 years as chief of the army, Sleiman also is believed to have unified the splintered military. However, he inherits a nation grappling with divisions. Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah. In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, triggering fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region. The election helped end a political crisis that deteriorated into violence this month. That crisis was defused when the Lebanese government gave in to two key Hezbollah demands -- lifting a government ban of Hezbollah's telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport. "The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah said. "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares - and unfortunately we must speak of shares - even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah's shares." Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli, and other Western targets and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. But many in Lebanon and other parts of the Middle East -- particularly Shiites -- view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

Nasrallah declared: "We do not seek to control Lebanon, to govern Lebanon, or to impose our ideas upon the Lebanese people, for we believe Lebanon to be a unique and diverse nation that requires the collaboration of all its citizens."

Nasrallah delivered these remarks a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman as the country's president, filling a post that had remained vacant for six months. Addressing his followers in a packed stadium, Nasrallah proclaimed: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a genuine national partnership, free of exclusions or impositions. The national unity government does not represent a victory of the opposition over the pro-government faction. Rather, it is a victory for all Lebanese."

He affirmed that Sleiman's election "renews the hope among the Lebanese people for a new era and a fresh beginning."

"I must acknowledge that there are deep wounds on both our side and theirs," he continued. "We are confronted with two choices: either to deepen these wounds and rub salt into them, or to strive to heal them for the sake of Lebanon. We choose the latter."

The parliament had attempted to elect a new president on 19 previous occasions, each failing amid disagreements over the distribution of power within a new Cabinet. Last week, Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached an agreement aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that had brought the country to the brink of civil war, thereby paving the way for Sleiman's election.

The accord, brokered in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government comprising a 30-member Cabinet -- 16 seats allocated to the majority, 11 to the Hezbollah-led opposition, and three reserved for the president's nomination. The allocation of seats had been a central point of contention for the opposition, which sought to secure the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will possess that authority.

In exchange for this veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end the sit-in protest that had paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006. In his address, Sleiman extended his gratitude to Qatar and the Arab League for their assistance in brokering the deal.

Sleiman emerged as the consensus candidate and is regarded as a neutral figure by Lebanon's political factions. The nation's previous presidents had been perceived as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. During his decade-long tenure as chief of the army, Sleiman is also credited with unifying the fragmented military. Nevertheless, he inherits a nation still grappling with profound divisions.

Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been embroiled in a power struggle with Hezbollah. Through public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah had threatened to leverage its power and popularity to unseat the Sunni-led government, stoking fears of a renewed civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region.

The election helped bring an end to a political crisis that had descended into violence earlier this month. That crisis was ultimately defused when the Lebanese government yielded to two of Hezbollah's key demands -- lifting a governmental ban on Hezbollah's telecommunications network and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport.

"The conduct of the opposition demonstrated that it did not orchestrate a coup, but merely sought the withdrawal of two decisions by the illegitimate government," Nasrallah stated. "I pledge that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal, and the Change and Reform bloc. We will grant other opposition parties their shares -- and, regrettably, we must speak in terms of shares -- even at the expense of Hezbollah's own."

Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against American, Israeli, and other Western targets, and the United States designates it as a terrorist organization. However, many across Lebanon and the broader Middle East -- particularly Shiites -- regard Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

# Hezbollah Chief Nasrallah Addresses Nation After Lebanon Elects President

Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah delivered a televised address following the election of army chief Michel Sleiman as Lebanon's new president, marking a significant turning point in the country's prolonged political crisis.

## End to Presidential Vacuum

Sleiman's election by parliament brought an end to a six-month presidential vacuum that had left Lebanon without a head of state and pushed the nation toward the brink of renewed sectarian conflict. The presidency had remained vacant since November 2007, when pro-Syrian President Emile Lahoud's term expired without agreement on a successor.

In his speech, Nasrallah struck a conciliatory tone, calling for national unity and cooperation with the newly elected president. The Hezbollah leader emphasized the importance of moving forward and rebuilding political consensus after months of paralysis.

## The Doha Agreement

The breakthrough came following negotiations in Doha, Qatar, where rival Lebanese factions reached a landmark deal brokered by Arab League mediators. The Doha agreement addressed several key points of contention:

- **Presidential election**: Clearing the way for Sleiman, a consensus candidate, to assume the presidency
- **National unity government**: Establishing a cabinet in which the opposition, led by Hezbollah, would receive veto power through 11 of 30 ministerial seats
- **Electoral law**: Setting terms for upcoming parliamentary elections
- **Weapons and violence**: Commitments to refrain from using force to achieve political gains

## Background to the Crisis

The political deadlock had escalated dramatically when the Western-backed government moved against Hezbollah's private telecommunications network and dismissed a security official at Beirut's airport. These decisions triggered violent clashes as Hezbollah fighters seized control of parts of Beirut, resulting in dozens of deaths in the worst internal fighting since Lebanon's civil war ended in 1990.

The confrontation heightened fears that Lebanon could descend into another prolonged sectarian conflict, prompting urgent regional intervention.

## Path Forward

Nasrallah's address signaled cautious optimism about Lebanon's political future while reaffirming Hezbollah's positions on key issues. The formation of the unity government and the presidential resolution represented a compromise among Lebanon's deeply divided factions, though significant challenges remained in fully implementing the terms of the Doha agreement.

The developments were closely watched by regional and international observers, given Lebanon's strategic importance and the involvement of external powers in the country's internal affairs.

---

# Hezbollah Chief Nasrallah Hails National Unity Following End to Presidential Deadlock

**BEIRUT** — Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah delivered remarks emphasizing national unity following the resolution of Lebanon's prolonged presidential vacuum, which had left the country without a head of state for approximately six months.

## Background of the Crisis

Lebanon had endured a significant political vacuum after President Émile Lahoud's term expired in November 2007. The parliament repeatedly failed to convene to elect a successor amid a deep standoff between the Western-backed March 14 governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition. The prolonged deadlock reflected broader tensions that had gripped the country following the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri and the subsequent withdrawal of Syrian forces.

The crisis reached a violent peak in May 2008, when clashes erupted in Beirut and other areas, raising fears of a return to the sectarian civil conflict that had devastated Lebanon between 1975 and 1990.

## The Doha Agreement

The breakthrough came through the Doha Agreement, brokered in Qatar, which produced a compromise among Lebanon's rival factions. The deal paved the way for the election of army commander General Michel Suleiman as president, a consensus candidate viewed as acceptable to both political camps.

The agreement also addressed the formation of a national unity government and disputes over electoral law, key sticking points that had fueled the political impasse.

## Nasrallah's Message

In his remarks, Nasrallah struck a conciliatory tone, framing the resolution as a victory for Lebanon as a whole rather than for any single faction. He emphasized themes of national reconciliation and the importance of dialogue among the country's diverse political and sectarian communities.

The Hezbollah leader stressed the need for cooperation among Lebanese factions to preserve stability and rebuild trust following the tense period. He characterized the outcome as an opportunity to move the country forward and away from the brink of renewed conflict.

## Significance

The end of the presidential vacancy marked a critical moment in Lebanese politics, temporarily easing sectarian tensions and restoring a degree of functionality to state institutions. Suleiman's election was widely welcomed by regional and international actors as a stabilizing development.

# Lebanon Breaks 18-Month Political Deadlock with Power-Sharing Cabinet Deal

*After a year and a half of paralysis that pushed the nation to the brink of renewed civil conflict, Lebanese factions have reached a compromise on Cabinet formation, with Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah pledging cooperation with the new government.*

---

**BEIRUT** — Lebanon's rival political camps announced a breakthrough agreement to end an 18-month political crisis that had paralyzed the country's governing institutions, threatened its fragile economy, and at times raised fears of a return to the sectarian violence that scarred the nation for decades.

The deal, brokered after marathon negotiations and significant regional mediation, establishes a national unity government built around a power-sharing formula that grants the opposition, led by Hezbollah, an effective veto over major Cabinet decisions. The compromise resolves the central sticking point that had frozen Lebanese politics and left the country without a functioning consensus at its highest levels.

## The Roots of the Crisis

The standoff had its origins in a deepening rift between the Western-backed governing coalition and an opposition bloc anchored by Hezbollah and its allies. The dispute centered on the distribution of Cabinet seats and, more consequentially, on which faction would hold the balance of power within the government.

At the heart of the disagreement was the opposition's demand for what became known as the "blocking third" — a share of Cabinet portfolios large enough to veto government decisions or force the Cabinet's collapse by resigning en masse. The governing majority resisted this demand for months, viewing it as an attempt to hamstring the government and undermine the results of previous elections.

The paralysis carried severe consequences. Government functions stalled, key appointments went unfilled, and the political vacuum bred instability that reverberated through Lebanon's markets and streets. The tension periodically boiled over into violence, deepening sectarian anxieties in a country where the memory of civil war remains vivid and the balance between communities is delicately calibrated.

## Terms of the Agreement

Under the new arrangement, Cabinet portfolios are distributed among the governing majority, the opposition, and a bloc of ministers aligned with the presidency. The formula effectively gives the opposition the leverage it had long sought, while allowing the majority to retain the largest share of seats and the premiership.

Officials involved in the talks described the outcome as a carefully balanced compromise — one in which neither side achieved total victory, but both secured enough to claim they had protected their core interests. Such arrangements are characteristic of Lebanon's consensus-driven, confessional political system, which apportions power among the country's religious communities and rewards negotiation over outright majoritarian rule.

The agreement paves the way for the formation of a national unity government intended to shepherd the country through a period of political and economic recovery, and to prepare for upcoming electoral and institutional processes.

## Nasrallah's Pledge

In a closely watched address, Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah welcomed the accord and pledged his movement's cooperation with the incoming government. He framed the agreement as a victory for national dialogue and a rejection of the paralysis that had gripped the country.

Nasrallah struck a conciliatory tone, calling on all Lebanese factions to turn the page on the confrontation and to prioritize the nation's stability. He signaled that his bloc would engage constructively within the new Cabinet, emphasizing partnership over obstruction — a message aimed at reassuring both domestic rivals and international observers wary of the movement's intentions.

The Hezbollah leader's remarks were significant precisely because his movement had been at the center of the standoff. His public commitment to cooperation represented an effort to lower the political temperature and to demonstrate that the compromise could hold in practice, not merely on paper.

## Regional and International Dimensions

The resolution did not emerge in isolation. Lebanon's internal disputes have long been entangled with broader regional rivalries, and the crisis reflected competing external interests as much as domestic ones. Diplomatic pressure and mediation from regional powers played a decisive role in nudging the factions toward compromise, underscoring how Lebanese politics remains permeable to outside influence.

The agreement was cautiously welcomed by international actors who had grown concerned that continued deadlock could destabilize an already volatile part of the Middle East. For Lebanon's foreign partners, a functioning government offered the prospect of renewed engagement on economic assistance and reform — leverage that had been difficult to apply while the country lacked a viable governing consensus.

## Cautious Optimism

While the breakthrough was greeted with relief across much of the country, analysts urged caution. Lebanon's history is replete with power-sharing arrangements that eased immediate crises only to sow the seeds of future ones. The very mechanisms that make compromise possible — the veto powers, the delicate confessional balance, the reliance on consensus — can also entrench gridlock and reward brinkmanship.

Observers noted that the deal addressed the symptoms of the crisis more than its underlying causes. The fundamental tensions between Lebanon's competing political and regional alignments remain, and the new government will have to navigate them while confronting pressing challenges, including economic strain, security concerns, and the persistent risk of sectarian friction.

For ordinary Lebanese, however, the end of the deadlock offered a measure of hope. After 18 months of uncertainty, the prospect of a functioning government — however fragile — represented a step back from the edge, and a chance to focus on the country's mounting practical problems rather than its political impasse.

Whether the spirit of cooperation invoked by Nasrallah and the other signatories will endure remains to be seen. In Lebanon, the formation of a government has often proved easier than the governing itself. The coming months will test whether the compromise marks a genuine turning point or merely a pause in the country's long-running political struggles.

---

*This article provides a general account of a Lebanese power-sharing resolution consistent with the patterns of the country's confessional politics. Readers seeking specific dates, names, and portfolio allocations should consult contemporaneous reporting for precise details.*

# Lebanon Elects Sleiman President, Ending Political Deadlock

**BEIRUT** — Lebanon's parliament elected army chief General Michel Sleiman as president on Sunday, filling a post that had been vacant for six months and ending a protracted political crisis that at times threatened to plunge the country back into civil conflict.

Sleiman, 59, secured the presidency with broad support from across Lebanon's fractured political spectrum, winning 118 of 127 votes cast in the 128-member legislature. His election came days after rival factions reached a power-sharing agreement in Doha, Qatar, brokered with the help of Arab League mediators.

## A Consensus Candidate

Widely regarded as a compromise figure acceptable to both the Western-backed governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition, Sleiman had commanded the army during a period in which the military largely maintained its position of neutrality amid deepening sectarian tensions.

In his inaugural address to parliament, Sleiman called for national unity and dialogue, urging Lebanese leaders to resolve their differences through political means rather than violence.

"The army will remain the guarantor of national unity and stability," Sleiman said, pledging to serve as a president for all Lebanese regardless of sect or political affiliation.

## The Doha Agreement

Sleiman's election was made possible by the accord reached in the Qatari capital, which resolved the central disputes that had paralyzed Lebanese politics. Under the terms of the deal, the opposition secured veto power in a new national unity government, a longstanding demand that had been a key sticking point in negotiations.

The agreement also established a framework for a new electoral law and called for an end to the sit-in protests that had occupied downtown Beirut. Critically, the parties agreed to refrain from the use of weapons to settle internal political disputes.

The breakthrough followed an outbreak of violence earlier this month, when clashes between rival factions left dozens dead and raised fears of a return to the sectarian warfare that devastated the country between 1975 and 1990.

## Hezbollah Reaction

Hezbollah officials welcomed the outcome, characterizing the agreement as a vindication of the opposition's position and a victory for its demands.

Representatives of the group praised the veto-guaranteeing provisions of the new government arrangement, describing the accord as a recognition of the movement's political weight within Lebanon. Opposition figures emphasized their commitment to the Doha framework while stressing that the agreement preserved what they characterized as legitimate rights of representation.

At the same time, Hezbollah leaders expressed support for Sleiman personally, reflecting the general's acceptability to the movement during his tenure as army commander.

## Looking Ahead

The challenges facing the new president remain formidable. Sleiman must now oversee the formation of the unity government and navigate the deep divisions that continue to define Lebanese politics, including fundamental disagreements over Hezbollah's arsenal and the country's regional alignments.

International reaction to the election was broadly positive, with regional and Western governments expressing hope that the resolution of the presidential vacuum would usher in a period of greater stability for the country.

For many ordinary Lebanese, weary of months of political paralysis and the recent bloodshed, the election offered a measure of cautious relief that the immediate crisis had been averted.
